about: Sourced life stories for the patriarchs and their households: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob (Israel), Rachel, Leah, Esau, Ishmael, Lot and Laban. Written from the KJV text of Genesis and the later verses that speak of them; no reviewed dossier exists for this group.

abraham-gen-11-26.short: Terah's son from Ur of the Chaldees, called by God to go to Canaan, renamed Abraham, father of Ishmael and Isaac.

paragraphs.text: Abram was a son of Terah, with brothers Nahor and Haran; Haran died in Ur of the Chaldees and left a son, Lot. Abram married Sarai, and "Sarai was barren; she had no child." Terah took Abram, Sarai and Lot out of Ur to go to Canaan, but they settled in Haran, and Terah died there. Joshua later says that Israel's fathers beyond the river, Terah among them, "served other gods".

The LORD told Abram to leave his country, his kindred and his father's house for "a land that I will shew thee", and promised to make of him a great nation: "in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed." He left Haran at seventy-five with Sarai, Lot and all they had, and came into Canaan. At Sichem the LORD promised the land to his seed, and Abram built altars there and near Beth-el. Stephen in Acts says God appeared to him in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.

In a famine Abram went down to Egypt and asked Sarai to say she was his sister, for fear the Egyptians would kill him and save her alive. She was taken into Pharaoh's house until the LORD plagued Pharaoh, who gave her back and sent them away. Back in Canaan, Abram and Lot had too many flocks to live together, so Abram let Lot choose, and Lot took the plain of Jordan. God then told Abram to look north, south, east and west: "all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it". Abram moved his tent to the plain of Mamre in Hebron.

When four kings carried Lot away from Sodom, Abram armed three hundred and eighteen servants born in his house, pursued them by night, and brought Lot and the goods back. Melchizedek king of Salem, "the priest of the most high God", brought out bread and wine and blessed Abram. Genesis says "he gave him tithes of all"; Hebrews says it was Abraham who gave him a tenth. Abram would take nothing of the king of Sodom's goods, "from a thread even to a shoelatchet".

Abram told God he was childless, that the steward of his house was Eliezer of Damascus, and that "one born in my house is mine heir". God brought him out to count the stars and said, "So shall thy seed be." "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Over the divided animals the LORD made a covenant with him to give the land to his seed. After ten years in Canaan, Sarai gave him her Egyptian maid Hagar, who bore him Ishmael when he was eighty-six.

When he was ninety-nine, God renamed him Abraham, "a father of many nations", renamed Sarai as Sarah, and gave circumcision as the token of the covenant. Abraham laughed at the promise of a son by Sarah, and that same day he circumcised Ishmael and all the men of his house. In the plains of Mamre the LORD appeared to him; he served a meal to three men, and was told that Sarah would have a son. When the LORD spoke of Sodom, Abraham asked, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?", and pleaded for the city from fifty righteous down to ten.

At Gerar Abraham again said of Sarah, "She is my sister", and Abimelech king of Gerar took her, until God warned him in a dream. So Genesis tells this of Abraham twice, in Egypt and in Gerar, and tells it once more of Isaac. Abraham told Abimelech she was "the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother". Isaac was born when Abraham was a hundred, and when Sarah asked him to cast out Hagar and her son, God told him to listen to her, and he sent them away with bread and water.

God told Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah; he bound Isaac on the altar, but the angel of the LORD called to him out of heaven, and he offered a ram instead, naming the place Jehovah-jireh. When Sarah died at Hebron, he bought the field and cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite for four hundred shekels and buried her there. After sending his servant to find Isaac a wife among his kindred, and taking another wife, Keturah, he died at a hundred and seventy-five, and Isaac and Ishmael buried him beside Sarah. James says he "was called the Friend of God", and Hebrews that he went out "not knowing whither he went".

sarah-gen-11-29.short: Abraham's wife, long barren, who went with him from Ur to Canaan, was renamed by God, and bore Isaac in her old age.

paragraphs.text: Sarai was Abram's wife, and "Sarai was barren; she had no child." She went with Abram and his father Terah from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran, and from there into Canaan. Abraham later said she was "the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother".

Genesis tells twice that Abraham called her his sister and that a king took her. In Egypt the Egyptians saw that she was "very fair", and she was taken into Pharaoh's house until the LORD plagued Pharaoh. At Gerar Abimelech king of Gerar took her, but God warned him in a dream, and he had not come near her; he gave her back with a thousand pieces of silver for her "brother".

After ten years in Canaan with no child, Sarai gave her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abram: "it may be that I may obtain children by her." When Hagar conceived and despised her, Sarai said to Abram, "My wrong be upon thee", and dealt hardly with Hagar, who fled.

God changed her name to Sarah and said she would be "a mother of nations". When a visitor at Mamre said she would have a son, she laughed within herself, being old, and then denied it, saying, "I laughed not", for she was afraid. The LORD asked, "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" She bore Isaac, and said, "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me."

After Isaac was weaned, Sarah saw Hagar's son mocking and told Abraham to cast out the bondwoman and her son, and God told him to listen to her. She died at a hundred and twenty-seven at Kirjath-arba, which is Hebron; Abraham wept for her and buried her in the cave of Machpelah. Isaac was comforted after her death when he brought Rebekah into her tent. Hebrews says she conceived "because she judged him faithful who had promised", and Peter's first letter that she obeyed Abraham, "calling him lord".

isaac-gen-17-19.short: The son promised to Abraham and Sarah in their old age, bound on the altar in Moriah, husband of Rebekah and father of Esau and Jacob.

paragraphs.text: God told Abraham that Sarah would bear him a son, "and thou shalt call his name Isaac", and that the covenant would be established with him. He was born when Abraham was a hundred, was circumcised on the eighth day, and Abraham made a great feast the day he was weaned. Sarah said, "God hath made me to laugh". When Sarah asked Abraham to cast out Hagar and Ishmael, God told him, "in Isaac shall thy seed be called."

God told Abraham to take "thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest" and offer him as a burnt offering in the land of Moriah. Isaac carried the wood and asked, "where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham answered, "God will provide himself a lamb". Abraham bound him and laid him on the altar, but the angel of the LORD called from heaven, and a ram was offered in his stead.

Abraham's servant went to the city of Nahor and brought back Rebekah, granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor. Isaac had gone out "to meditate in the field at the eventide" when the camels came; he brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, "and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death." He was forty. With Ishmael he buried Abraham in the cave of Machpelah, and he lived by the well Lahai-roi.

Rebekah was barren until Isaac prayed for her; she bore twins, Esau and Jacob, when he was sixty, and "Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison". In a famine the LORD told him not to go down into Egypt and renewed to him the oath sworn to Abraham. At Gerar he said Rebekah was his sister, as Genesis tells twice of Abraham and Sarah, until Abimelech king of the Philistines saw him with her and charged his people not to touch them. He sowed and reaped a hundredfold, dug again his father's wells, and after strife over two wells, dug a third and called it Rehoboth: "the LORD hath made room for us".

At Beer-sheba the LORD appeared to him, and he built an altar there, and Abimelech came to make a covenant with him. Esau's Hittite wives "were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah". When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim, he meant to bless Esau, but Jacob came in Esau's clothes and received the blessing; when Esau came, Isaac "trembled very exceedingly". He then sent Jacob to Padan-aram to take a wife from the daughters of Laban.

Jacob came back to him at Mamre, which is Hebron. Isaac died at a hundred and eighty, "old and full of days", and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him; Jacob later said Isaac and Rebekah were buried in the cave of Machpelah. Hebrews says, "By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come."

rebekah-gen-22-23.short: Daughter of Bethuel and sister of Laban, who left her family to marry Isaac, bore Esau and Jacob, and won Isaac's blessing for Jacob.

paragraphs.text: Rebekah was the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Abraham's brother Nahor and Milcah, and Laban was her brother. Abraham's servant waited by the well outside the city of Nahor and prayed that the girl who offered to water his camels would be the one appointed for Isaac. Before he had finished, Rebekah came with her pitcher, gave him a drink and said, "I will draw water for thy camels also". He gave her a gold earring and two bracelets.

Laban and Bethuel said, "The thing proceedeth from the LORD". Her brother and mother asked that she stay at least ten days, but when they asked her, she said, "I will go." She left with her nurse and her damsels, and her family blessed her: "be thou the mother of thousands of millions". When she saw Isaac in the field she covered herself with a vail, and he brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, "and he loved her".

Rebekah was barren until Isaac prayed for her. The twins struggled within her, and she went to ask the LORD, who told her, "Two nations are in thy womb" and "the elder shall serve the younger." Esau was born first and Jacob after, and "Rebekah loved Jacob." Paul in Romans repeats the word spoken to her before the children were born.

At Gerar Isaac said she was his sister, because she "was fair to look upon", until Abimelech saw Isaac with her. Esau's Hittite wives were a grief to her and to Isaac. When she heard Isaac send Esau for venison so he could bless him, she had Jacob fetch two kids, made the savoury meat, dressed him in Esau's clothes and covered his hands with the skins. When Jacob feared a curse, she said, "Upon me be thy curse, my son".

Told that Esau meant to kill Jacob, she sent Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran for "a few days", saying, "why should I be deprived also of you both in one day?" She told Isaac she was weary of her life because of the daughters of Heth, and Isaac sent Jacob to Padan-aram for a wife. Genesis does not tell of her death. It records that her nurse Deborah died and was buried below Beth-el, and Jacob said at his death that Rebekah was buried with Isaac in the cave of Machpelah.

israel-gen-25-26.short: Isaac's younger twin, who took Esau's birthright and blessing, served Laban for Leah and Rachel, was renamed Israel, and died in Egypt.

paragraphs.text: Jacob was the younger of Isaac and Rebekah's twins; he was born with his hand holding Esau's heel. Esau became a hunter, while Jacob was "a plain man, dwelling in tents", and "Rebekah loved Jacob." When Esau came in faint from the field, Jacob made him swear away his birthright for bread and pottage of lentiles.

Following Rebekah's plan, Jacob came in Esau's clothes to his father, whose eyes were dim, and said, "I am Esau thy firstborn", and received the blessing. Esau said in his heart that when the days of mourning for their father came he would kill him, so Rebekah sent him to Laban, and Isaac blessed him again and charged him to take a wife there. On the way he dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, with the angels of God on it and the LORD above it, promising him the land and saying, "I am with thee". He named the place Beth-el and vowed that if God kept him and brought him home, the LORD would be his God.

At a well near Haran he met Rachel, the daughter of his mother's brother Laban, rolled the stone from the well, kissed her and wept. He served Laban seven years for her, "and they seemed unto him but a few days", but Laban gave him Leah first and Rachel a week later for seven more years. Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and a daughter, Dinah; Rachel's maid Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali, and Leah's maid Zilpah bore Gad and Asher. At last Rachel bore Joseph.

Jacob agreed to take the speckled and spotted beasts as his wages, set peeled rods before the stronger flocks, and grew very rich. When Laban's face turned against him, the LORD told him to return home, and he left without telling Laban; Rachel had stolen her father's images. Laban overtook him in mount Gilead, and Jacob said, "This twenty years have I been with thee", adding that Laban had changed his wages ten times. They set up a heap of stones as a witness between them, and Laban kissed and blessed his daughters and their children and went home.

Told that Esau was coming with four hundred men, Jacob "was greatly afraid and distressed", prayed, and sent droves of animals ahead as a present. Left alone by the ford Jabbok, he wrestled with a man until daybreak, who touched the hollow of his thigh and said, "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel". He called the place Peniel, "for I have seen God face to face", and he limped on his thigh. Esau ran to meet him and embraced him, and they wept. Hosea says of him, "he had power over the angel, and prevailed".

Jacob bought land at Shechem; there Dinah was defiled by Shechem son of Hamor, Simeon and Levi killed the men of the city, and Jacob told them they had made him "to stink among the inhabitants of the land". God sent him to Beth-el, appeared to him again and said, "thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name", so Genesis tells of his new name twice, at Peniel and at Beth-el. On the way to Ephrath Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin, and Jacob set a pillar on her grave. Jacob came to his father Isaac at Hebron, and he and Esau buried Isaac.

Israel loved Joseph more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours; when his sons brought the coat dipped in blood, he mourned and "refused to be comforted". In the famine he sent ten sons to Egypt for corn but kept Benjamin back, and let him go only when he had to: "If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved." Told that Joseph was alive and governor of Egypt, he said, "It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive". At Beer-sheba God told him, "fear not to go down into Egypt", and he went down with all his house; Joseph met him in Goshen, and before Pharaoh Jacob said his years had been a hundred and thirty.

Jacob lived seventeen years in Egypt and died at a hundred and forty-seven. He made Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers, took Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, crossing his hands to set the younger first, and gathered his sons to bless them. He was embalmed, the Egyptians mourned him seventy days, and his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah; Hebrews recalls that he blessed Joseph's sons "leaning upon the top of his staff". Most verses on this record name the nation Israel, the people descended from him, not the man himself.

rachel-gen-29-6.short: Laban's younger daughter, whom Jacob loved and served fourteen years for; long barren, she bore Joseph and died giving birth to Benjamin.

paragraphs.text: Rachel was the younger daughter of Laban and kept her father's sheep. Jacob met her at the well, watered her flock, kissed her and wept, and told her he was Rebekah's son. "Rachel was beautiful and well favoured", and Jacob served seven years for her, but Laban gave him Leah first, and Rachel a week later, with Bilhah as her maid, for seven more years of service.

Rachel was barren while Leah bore sons; she envied her sister and said to Jacob, "Give me children, or else I die." She gave him her maid Bilhah, and named Bilhah's sons Dan and Naphtali, saying, "With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister". She gave Leah a night with Jacob in exchange for Reuben's mandrakes. Then "God remembered Rachel", and she bore Joseph, saying, "The LORD shall add to me another son."

When Jacob decided to leave, Rachel and Leah agreed, saying, "Are we not counted of him strangers?" Rachel stole her father's images; when Laban searched her tent, she sat on them in the camel's furniture and said she could not rise before him. Jacob, not knowing she had taken them, had said that whoever had them should not live. When Esau came to meet them, Jacob put Rachel and Joseph last.

On the way to Ephrath she had hard labour; as she died she named her son Ben-oni, but his father called him Benjamin. She was buried on the way to Ephrath, "which is Beth-lehem", and Jacob set a pillar on her grave; in Egypt he spoke of her death to Joseph. Samuel later speaks of "Rachel's sepulchre in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah".

At Bethlehem the elders wished that Ruth would be "like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel". In Jeremiah the LORD tells of a voice in Ramah, "Rahel weeping for her children", and Matthew says that word was fulfilled when Herod had the children of Bethlehem killed.

leah-gen-29-16.short: Laban's elder daughter, given to Jacob in Rachel's place; mother of six of his sons and of Dinah, and buried at Machpelah.

paragraphs.text: Leah was the elder daughter of Laban: "Leah was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured." After Jacob had served seven years for Rachel, Laban brought Leah to him in the evening instead, with Zilpah as her maid. In the morning Jacob asked, "wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban answered that in their country the younger was not given before the firstborn.

Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and "when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb". Her words at the births speak of the LORD and of her husband: with Reuben, "now therefore my husband will love me"; with Simeon, that the LORD had heard "that I was hated"; with Levi, "Now this time will my husband be joined unto me"; and with Judah, "Now will I praise the LORD."

When she stopped bearing, she gave Jacob her maid Zilpah, who bore Gad and Asher. In exchange for her son Reuben's mandrakes, Rachel gave her a night with Jacob, and she bore Issachar and then Zebulun, saying, "now will my husband dwell with me". Afterwards she bore a daughter, Dinah.

She agreed with Rachel that Jacob should leave their father, who, they said, "hath sold us". Laban searched her tent for his images and did not find them. When Esau came, Leah and her children went before Rachel. Her daughter Dinah was later defiled at Shechem.

Genesis does not tell of her death; at his own death Jacob said that in the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham and Sarah and Isaac and Rebekah lay, "there I buried Leah". At Bethlehem the people and the elders spoke of Rachel and Leah, "which two did build the house of Israel".

esau-gen-25-25.short: Isaac's elder twin, a hunter who sold his birthright for pottage, lost the blessing to Jacob, later embraced him, and settled in mount Seir.

paragraphs.text: Esau was the first of the twins born to Isaac and Rebekah, "red, all over like an hairy garment". He became "a cunning hunter, a man of the field", and Isaac loved him because he ate of his venison. Coming in faint from the field, he asked Jacob for the red pottage, "therefore was his name called Edom", and sold him his birthright with an oath. The text says, "thus Esau despised his birthright."

At forty he married Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, who "were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah". Seeing that the daughters of Canaan did not please his father, he also married Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael. Genesis lists his wives a second time with different names: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, and Bashemath, Ishmael's daughter. The text does not explain the difference between the two lists.

Isaac sent him to hunt venison so that he could bless him, but Jacob came first and took the blessing. When Esau heard, "he cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry", and said, "Bless me, even me also, O my father." Isaac told him that he would live by his sword and serve his brother, until he broke his brother's yoke from his neck. Esau hated Jacob and said that when the days of mourning for his father came, he would kill him.

Years later, living in Seir, Esau came to meet Jacob with four hundred men. He ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him, and they wept. He said, "I have enough, my brother", but took Jacob's present when Jacob urged him, and went back to Seir. He and Jacob buried their father Isaac.

Esau took his household and cattle away from Jacob into mount Seir, because the land could not bear them both: "Esau is Edom." Genesis calls him "the father of the Edomites", and Deuteronomy says the LORD gave mount Seir to Esau for a possession. Some verses on this record, in Deuteronomy, Obadiah and elsewhere, name the people descended from him, "the children of Esau" or "the house of Esau", not the man himself. Hebrews remembers him as one "who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright".

ishmael-gen-16-11.short: Abraham's son by Hagar the Egyptian, sent away with his mother, who grew up an archer in the wilderness and fathered twelve princes.

paragraphs.text: Hagar, Sarai's Egyptian maid, fled after Sarai dealt hardly with her. The angel of the LORD found her by a fountain on the way to Shur, sent her back, and told her she would bear a son, "and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction." He said the boy would be "a wild man; his hand will be against every man". Ishmael was born when Abram was eighty-six.

When God promised Abraham a son by Sarah, Abraham said, "O that Ishmael might live before thee!" God answered that he had blessed Ishmael and would make him a great nation, the father of twelve princes, but that he would establish his covenant with Isaac. Ishmael was circumcised at thirteen, on the same day as Abraham.

After Isaac was weaned, Sarah saw Ishmael mocking and asked Abraham to cast him and his mother out. The thing was grievous to Abraham "because of his son", but God told him to listen to Sarah and promised to make a nation of Ishmael too. Sent away with bread and water, Hagar left the boy under a shrub when the water was gone; God heard the voice of the lad and opened her eyes to a well of water. "God was with the lad"; he grew up in the wilderness of Paran and became an archer, and his mother took him a wife out of Egypt.

Ishmael and Isaac buried Abraham in the cave of Machpelah. His twelve sons, beginning with Nebajoth and Kedar, were "twelve princes according to their nations", and his daughter Mahalath married Esau. He lived a hundred and thirty-seven years and "died in the presence of all his brethren". Paul writes in Galatians that Abraham had two sons, "the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman".

lot-gen-11-27.short: Abraham's nephew, the son of Haran, who went with him to Canaan, settled near Sodom, and was brought out before its destruction.

paragraphs.text: Lot was the son of Haran, who died in Ur of the Chaldees; his grandfather Terah took him with Abram toward Canaan, and he went on with Abram from Haran. When their flocks grew too great for the land and their herdmen quarrelled, Abram let Lot choose where to go. Lot chose the well-watered plain of Jordan and pitched his tent toward Sodom, whose men "were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly."

When four kings defeated the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, they took Lot, who was living in Sodom, and his goods. Abram pursued them with his servants and brought Lot back with his goods and the people.

Two angels came to Sodom in the evening; Lot was sitting in the gate, pressed them to stay with him, and made them a feast. The men of the city surrounded the house and demanded the visitors; Lot went out, shut the door behind him, and offered them his two daughters instead. The visitors pulled him back inside and struck the men at the door with blindness. When Lot warned his sons-in-law to leave, "he seemed as one that mocked" to them.

At dawn, while he lingered, the men took Lot, his wife and his two daughters by the hand, "the LORD being merciful unto him", and set them outside the city. Lot asked to flee to a little city nearby rather than to the mountain, and it was called Zoar. The LORD rained brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt. Genesis says that God "remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow".

Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot lived in a cave in the mountain with his two daughters. On two nights they made him drink wine and lay with him, and he did not know it; the elder bore Moab, father of the Moabites, and the younger Ben-ammi, father of the children of Ammon. Genesis tells nothing more of Lot, not even his death. Deuteronomy says the LORD gave land to "the children of Lot", in Luke Jesus said, "Remember Lot's wife", and Peter's second letter calls him "just Lot".

laban-gen-24-29.short: Rebekah's brother and father of Leah and Rachel, who gave Rebekah to Isaac and had Jacob serve him for twenty years.

paragraphs.text: Laban was Rebekah's brother, and Genesis calls him "Laban the Syrian". When he saw the earring and bracelets on his sister, he ran out to Abraham's servant at the well and said, "Come in, thou blessed of the LORD". He and Bethuel answered, "The thing proceedeth from the LORD", and he and his mother asked that Rebekah stay at least ten days before she went.

Rebekah later sent Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran. Jacob asked the shepherds there for "Laban the son of Nahor"; Laban ran to meet him and said, "Surely thou art my bone and my flesh." He agreed to seven years' service for his younger daughter Rachel, but brought Leah to Jacob instead, and when Jacob protested he said, "It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn." He gave Rachel too, for seven more years, with Zilpah and Bilhah as maids for his daughters.

When Jacob asked to leave, Laban said, "the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake", and asked him to name his wages. Jacob took the speckled and spotted beasts, and Laban's sons complained that Jacob had taken all that was their father's. Jacob told his wives that Laban had changed his wages ten times, and Rachel and Leah said their father "hath sold us".

Laban was away shearing his sheep when Jacob fled and Rachel stole his images. He pursued for seven days, but God came to him in a dream: "Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad." He searched the tents and did not find his gods. They set up a heap of stones as a witness, which Laban called Jegar-sahadutha and Jacob Galeed, and Laban said, "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." In the morning he "kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them", and went home; Genesis tells nothing more of him.
